name: Plan and schedule a planned thermal unit outage
summary: This process turns a planned outage in the multi-year plan into a ready-to-run outage: scope, job plans, contractor awards, long-lead parts, a critical-path schedule, a safety and isolation plan and a budget. It covers the converted gas units and cogeneration plants; hydro and wind unit outages are planned inside their own divisions. Outage managers and planners in the engineering division do most of the work with reliability engineers, plant maintenance planners, the plant manager and the trading desk. It is slow because planning starts 6 to 18 months ahead, contractor tenders and long-lead parts take months, and dates move when prices, the AESO or late parts force a reschedule.

baseline.org_archetype: An Alberta merchant generator with about 1,300 staff, three gas steam units converted from coal at the Wabamun-area sites, two cogeneration plants, 17 hydro plants and 12 wind farms, with a central engineering and asset management division of about 130 people.
baseline.notes: Reference period 2019 to 2022. In 2019-2020 the Wabamun-area units still burned coal, and three boiler conversions were done during planned outages in 2020-2021; those conversions are planned by the energy transition division but share outage windows with this process.

unit_of_work: one planned thermal or cogeneration unit outage (major or minor)
trigger: The annual capital plan confirms an outage for a unit in the coming years.
end_state: The outage plan (scope, schedule, budget, safety plan) is issued to the execution team, or the outage is deferred.

volume.seasonality: Plans are issued ahead of the April-June and September-November outage seasons.

evidence.note: TransAlta reported two planned major outages on its Alberta coal units in 2019, one (non-operated) in 2018 and four in 2017 (tac2019mda). With three converted units on annual minor outages, two cogeneration plants and one or two majors a year, about 8 to 12 thermal outages a year are planned. The organisation file's 1/4/10 per month counts hydro and wind unit outages, which this group does not plan in detail.
Four outage managers; about 40 percent of their time on planning, the rest on execution and AESO reporting.
Twelve planners; about 40 percent on thermal outage planning, the rest on hydro support, AESO reporting and execution.
Plant maintenance planners write outage job plans; not listed in the organisation file's roles for this process.
Scope recommendations for each outage.
Pressure equipment inspection scope; not listed in the organisation file's roles for this process.
Scope review and freeze.
Outage safety plan; not listed in the organisation file's roles for this process.
Isolation lists; not listed in the organisation file's roles for this process.
Budget approval for major outages.
Concurs with major outage budgets; takes no separate step in this file.

systems.name: Outage and project scheduling software (critical path)
ERP (finance, purchasing and plant maintenance modules)
AESO Energy Trading System (offers, declarations and dispatch)
Document management and engineering drawings repository

steps.name: Place outage in long-range outage plan
steps.description: The outage manager opens the multi-year outage plan in the scheduling tool and the capital plan spreadsheet, takes the OEM inspection intervals (operating hours and starts since the last major) and the capital items that need the unit offline, and sets the season, year and planned duration for the outage. They check that no two Wabamun-area units or both cogeneration trains are planned out together.

error.defect_description: Duration or season set without checking an overlapping unit or a conversion project.

evidence.note: Common practice at thermal generators; the annual capital plan is the trigger in the organisation file.

steps.name: Agree outage window with trading desk
steps.description: The outage manager meets the portfolio optimisation analysts, compares the proposed window with the forward price curve and other planned outages in the province, and moves the outage into the spring or fall shoulder season when prices are usually lower. The agreed window is recorded in the plan.

evidence.note: Merchant generators in an energy-only market place outages in low-price seasons; the TransAlta 2019 MD&A describes moving outages for price reasons at another plant (not cited for this step).

steps.name: Add outage to monthly 24-month AESO submission
steps.description: The outage planner adds the outage dates, MW impact, type (Outage-Planned or Derate-Planned) and nature of work to the list for the monthly submission, which the outage reporting process enters in the AESO Energy Trading System by the first of the month. Every planned outage in the next 24 months must be on it.

error.defect_description: Wrong MW impact or dates typed into the submission list.

evidence.note: ISO rule 306.5 s.3(2): monthly submission of planned outages within the next 24 months.

steps.name: Gather scope inputs when planning starts
steps.description: When the outage reaches its planning start (about 12 to 18 months ahead for a major, 6 months for a minor), the outage planner pulls from the ERP every deferred work order flagged as outage-only, open work requests, the last outage report, OEM technical bulletins and the pressure equipment inspection due list, and builds a draft scope list in a spreadsheet.

error.defect_description: Outage-only work orders missed because they were not flagged in the ERP.

evidence.note: Planning is continuous and major outages are planned well ahead (powermag2014); the 12-18 and 6 month planning starts are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Travel to plant for scope walkdown
steps.description: The outage planner drives a company truck from the engineering office to the plant site, signs in at the gate and collects a site radio and permit-area briefing before walking the unit.

evidence.note: Engineering staff are based at an office away from the Wabamun-area plants; one to four hours of driving each way is assumed.

steps.name: Walk down equipment and confirm scope
steps.description: The outage planner walks the boiler, turbine deck and auxiliaries with the maintenance supervisor, checks each scope item in the field, notes access needs (scaffold, insulation removal, crane reach) and photographs equipment, then marks items to add or drop on the draft scope list.

evidence.note: Common planning practice; walkdowns verify access and scope before job plans are written.

steps.name: Review condition data and recommend inspection scope
steps.description: The reliability engineer reviews historian trends (vibration, bearing temperatures, heat rate), boiler tube leak history, past NDE results and failure reports, and recommends which inspections, replacements and upgrades belong in this outage. Items needing parts with long delivery times are flagged.

error.defect_description: A degraded component not put in scope; found as discovered work during execution.

evidence.note: Condition-based scoping by reliability engineers is common practice; hours estimated.

steps.name: Write job plans and work orders
steps.description: For each scope item the maintenance planner writes a job plan in the ERP plant maintenance module: steps, trades and hours, parts and reservations, special tools, isolation points and hold points. A major outage has several hundred work orders; a minor outage has under a hundred.

error.defect_description: Missing parts or steps in job plans.

evidence.note: Work order counts and hours per job plan estimated from common thermal plant practice.

steps.name: Review and freeze outage scope
steps.description: The plant manager chairs the scope review with planners, engineering and maintenance supervisors, challenges each item against cost and risk, removes or defers items and freezes the scope list. Later additions must go through scope change control.

control.basis: Outage scope freeze and scope change control procedure

next.condition: outage deferred or folded into a conversion or retirement

evidence.note: Early scope freeze before contractor estimating (powermag2014); branch shares are estimates: major outages every 3 to 6 years per unit against annual minors.

steps.name: Raise material requests for long-lead parts
steps.description: The outage planner raises material requests in the ERP for long-lead items such as turbine blades, valve internals, boiler tube panels and generator parts, attaching specifications and OEM quotes, so supply chain can order them 6 to 12 months ahead.

error.defect_description: Wrong part number or revision on a material request.

evidence.note: Long-lead parts named as a typical readiness risk (powermag2014); hours estimated.

steps.name: Prepare contractor scope packages
steps.description: The outage planner writes scope packages for boiler repair, scaffolding, insulation, turbine OEM services and NDE, with quantities, schedule windows and safety requirements, and sends them to supply chain as service orders for tender.

error.defect_description: Package omits work, leading to change orders during execution.

evidence.note: Contractors estimate and schedule after scope freeze (powermag2014).

steps.name: Evaluate contractor bids technically
steps.description: After supply chain runs the tender, the outage manager scores each bid for manpower plan, schedule, safety record and exclusions, asks bidders clarifying questions and recommends an award.

evidence.note: Tender periods of one to four months for outage services are an estimate.

steps.name: Build major outage cost estimate
steps.description: The outage manager builds the outage budget from job plan hours, contractor bids, material costs, crane rental and a contingency for discovered work, and compares it with the capital plan amount for the outage.

error.defect_description: Contingency too low for discovered work.

evidence.note: Planned major maintenance of 34 million CAD for two major coal outages in 2019 (tac2019mda) indicates budgets of 10 to 20 million CAD per major outage.

steps.name: Approve major outage budget
steps.description: The vice-president of engineering, with the vice-president of gas generation, reviews the budget, schedule, risks and expected availability gain and approves it under the delegation of authority, or asks for cuts.

evidence.note: Delegation of authority approval for spend of this size is common practice.

steps.name: Estimate minor outage and raise requests
steps.description: For a minor outage the outage planner prices the work from job plans, raises material requests and service orders for the few contractors needed, and sends the estimate to the plant manager for sign-off within the plant's maintenance budget.

evidence.note: Minor outages are funded from plant budgets in common practice.

steps.name: Build critical-path schedule
steps.description: The outage planner loads work orders into the critical-path scheduling tool, links logic (cool-down, isolation, scaffold, open, inspect, repair, close, test), sets the two-shift calendar and resource limits for crews and cranes, and finds the critical path, which for a major runs through the turbine.

error.defect_description: Logic or durations wrong, so the critical path is understated.

evidence.note: Critical-path scheduling of outages is common practice; hours estimated.

steps.name: Request specialist crews and cranes
steps.description: The outage planner sends a crew request to the specialist crew booking process for turbine, valve and rigging crews and the mobile cranes on the scheduled dates, and checks the reply against other sites' bookings.

evidence.note: Four shared specialist crews and two owned cranes in the organisation file must be booked across sites.

steps.name: Review outage safety plan
steps.description: The safety advisor reviews the high-risk work in the schedule (boiler confined-space entry, critical lifts, scaffolding, hot work and the peak number of contractors on site) and sets the orientation, rescue and supervision requirements in the outage safety plan.

control.basis: Alberta OHS Act and Code (hazard assessment, confined space, lifting); company outage safety standard

evidence.note: Outage safety planning is common practice; safety advisors are shared across sites, so the wait reflects their availability.

steps.name: Prepare isolation lists
steps.description: A shift supervisor uses the drawings and the permit-to-work system to list every isolation point (valves, breakers, drains and vents) for each system in the outage, so that permits can be issued quickly once the unit is shut down.

error.defect_description: Isolation point missing from a list.

control.basis: Alberta OHS Code Part 15 ss. 212-214 control of hazardous energy

evidence.note: Hazardous energy must be isolated and verified before work (ohs15); hours estimated.

steps.name: Send pressure equipment inspection scope
steps.description: The plant engineer sends the outage dates and the list of boilers, vessels and piping due for inspection to the pressure equipment inspection process, so inspectors and NDE contractors can be booked within the outage window.
outputs: outage plan for pressure equipment inspection

control.basis: Alberta Pressure Equipment Safety Regulation and the owner's ABSA-accepted integrity management program

evidence.note: Boilers and pressure vessels are inspected under ABSA rules during outages; the organisation file links this process to inspection.

steps.name: Hold outage readiness review
steps.description: The outage manager holds readiness reviews at about 90, 60 and 30 days before shutdown, going through parts delivery, contractor mobilisation, work package completeness and permits, and codes each item green, yellow or red. Red items go on the risk register with a contingency.

next.condition: dates moved by the market, the AESO or late parts

evidence.note: 90/60/30-day readiness meetings with green/yellow/red coding (powermag2014); branch shares estimated.

steps.name: Chase late parts and contractor gaps
steps.description: The outage planner calls buyers, suppliers and contractors about red items, gets revised delivery dates, finds substitute parts or resequences work, and updates the readiness tracker before the next review.

evidence.note: Chasing long-lead items is the usual response to red readiness items.

steps.name: Confirm final dates and update AESO submission
steps.description: The outage planner confirms the final shutdown and return dates with the trading desk and passes them to the outage reporting process for the ETS update. A change within 3 months of the start needs a written reason in the submission.

steps.name: Issue outage plan to execution
steps.description: The outage manager issues the final outage plan (scope, schedule, budget, safety plan, contractor list, isolation lists) at a handover meeting with the execution team and plant operations about two weeks before shutdown.

evidence.note: Formal handover from planning to execution is common practice.

exceptions.name: Outage moved after scheduling
exceptions.description: The trading desk, an AESO adequacy concern or a late long-lead part moves the outage dates, so the schedule is rebuilt and the AESO submission revised with a statement of reasons.

exceptions.name: Red readiness items
exceptions.description: Parts or contractor mobilisation are not ready at a readiness review and must be chased before the next review.

exceptions.name: Outage deferred
exceptions.description: The outage is deferred at scope freeze or budget approval, often because the unit is being converted or retired.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from capital plan confirmation to outage plan issue
benchmarks.population: Planned thermal outages at an Alberta generator, 2019-2022

evidence.note: Author's estimate: the annual capital plan confirms minor outages 6 to 12 months before they start and majors 18 to 24 months before (they must already sit in the AESO 24-month submission); the plan is issued about two weeks before shutdown. With about three minors to each major the median is about a year. powermag2014 says major outages are planned years ahead but gives no figure.

benchmarks.population: Alberta generating assets of 5 MW or more

evidence.note: ISO rule 306.5 s.3(2).
34 million CAD of Canadian Coal planned major maintenance across two planned major outages in 2019; the division is the author's.

pain_points.description: Long-lead parts and contractor tenders set the planning start; a late material request turns into a red readiness item or a moved outage.

evidence.note: Long-lead parts are named as typical red items.

pain_points.description: Job plans for several hundred work orders are written by hand in the ERP by a few plant planners who also plan routine work, so outage job plans queue behind daily work.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice.

pain_points.description: Scope missed in planning appears as discovered work during the outage and drives overruns.

evidence.note: Scope creep and emergent work named as the main threat.

pain_points.description: Dates set in the AESO 24-month submission are moved when prices or adequacy change, and every change within 3 months needs a written reason.

assumptions: Scope is the converted gas units and cogeneration plants. Hydro and wind unit outages are planned by those divisions and only reported through eng-report-outages-aeso; this explains the lower volume than the organisation file.
Loaded costs are taken from the organisation file (wage x 1.40).
Touch times are the hours of the named role on one outage. Major outages (about a quarter of cases) carry most of the hours; the branch at s09 separates the two paths.
The simulated cycle starts when the capital plan confirms the outage, so most elapsed time is the calendar wait before planning starts (s04).
AESO ETS entries are made in eng-report-outages-aeso; this file passes dates to it at s03 and s23.
The maintenance_planner role is in the organisation file but not in this process's role list; it is used here because plant planners write outage job plans.

The simulated median (about 440 days) is about 1.2 times the 365-day benchmark. The simulator draws each step independently, so minor outages also pick up long planning-start waits meant for majors; the model's spread between minor and major outages is narrower than in practice.

sources.title: ISO Rules Section 306.5 Generation Outage Reporting and Coordination (effective 2023-01-01; revision history back to 2014)
sources.supports: Pool participants with assets of 5 MW or more must, by the first day of every month, submit through the Energy Trading System all planned outages expected in the next 24 months (dates, MW impact, nature of work, Derate-Planned or Outage-Planned); revisions as soon as reasonably practicable; changes later than 3 months before the start need a statement of reasons; the ISO may direct cancellation of a planned outage for adequacy or reliability after a posting of at least one week, and not more than 90 days ahead of the shortfall. The 2020-09-16 and 2023-01-01 revisions did not change the planned outage requirements.

sources.title: Critical Path: Getting Your Outage Ducks in a Row (A. Larson)
sources.supports: Outage preparation is continuous and can be a full-time department; major projects are planned years ahead; scope is frozen early and contractors estimate and schedule only after the freeze; readiness meetings 90, 60 and 30 days before shutdown with tasks coded green, yellow or red; long-lead parts are a typical red item; unready tasks go on a risk register; scope creep and emergent work are the main threat.

sources.title: TransAlta Corporation Management's Discussion and Analysis for 2019 (Exhibit 13.2 to Form 40-F)
sources.publisher: TransAlta Corporation via U.S. SEC EDGAR
sources.supports: Canadian Coal planned major maintenance 34 million CAD in 2019, 15 million in 2018, 54 million in 2017; two planned major outages (Keephills 1 and Sundance 4) in 2019, one planned major outage at a non-operated unit in 2018 and four planned outages in 2017; Canadian Gas planned major maintenance 8, 16 and 22 million; consolidated sustaining capital 141 million CAD (2019), 150 million (2018), 218 million (2017) and 170 to 200 million forecast for 2020.

sources.title: Occupational Health and Safety Code, Part 15 Managing the Control of Hazardous Energy (Alberta Regulation 191/2021)
sources.supports: Part 15 requires isolation of machinery and equipment before work (s. 212), verification of isolation (s. 213), personal locks (s. 214) and rules for securing by individual workers and groups. The same Part existed in the earlier Code (AR 87/2009) in force in 2019 to 2021.
